title: Linear for Executives: How to Stay on Top of It
summary: A practical guide to Linear for executives: 7 ways to track engineering progress, spot blockers early and stay informed without living in Linear.
body_markdown:
Using Linear for executives is a strange problem. Linear is where your product and engineering teams actually work, so it holds the truest picture of what's shipping, what's late and what's stuck. But it's built for the people doing the work, not the people steering it. Open it on a busy morning and you're looking at hundreds of issues, cycles and comments.


So most leaders end up in one of two places. Either they live in Linear and get pulled into the weeds, or they stay out of it and rely on secondhand status updates that arrive a week late.


There's a better middle ground. Here's how to get the signal from Linear without drowning in it.


## Key takeaways


-


Track work at the **initiative and project level** , not the issue level.


-


Let **project updates and Pulse** bring the news to you on a schedule you choose.


-


Connect Linear to a tool like **BOND** so the few issues that need you show up next to your email, Slack and meetings.


## 1. Zoom out to initiatives


Linear's Initiatives group projects around company goals, like "Launch enterprise tier" or "Cut onboarding time in half." Each initiative has an owner, a target date and a status, and it rolls up the health of every project underneath it.


For an executive, this is the right altitude. Instead of scanning issues, you can look at one view and see which goals are on track and which aren't. Linear color-codes project health in the Initiatives view: green for on track, yellow for at risk, red for off track, and gray when there's no recent update.


If your team doesn't use initiatives yet, ask them to set up three to five that map to your company's real priorities. It's the single biggest change you can make to how useful Linear is for you.


## 2. Make project updates the habit


Project health in Linear comes from project updates, short written check-ins where the project lead marks the work as on track, at risk or off track and explains why.


Those updates are your best source of truth, but only if they happen regularly. Agree on a cadence with your team (weekly works for most), and make it clear that "at risk" is a welcome signal, not a failure. An honest yellow this week beats a surprise red next month.


Gray matters too. A project with no recent update is often the one that needs attention. Linear's own guidance for leaders is to mention the project lead and check for missed updates or blockers.


## 3. Let Pulse bring the updates to you


You shouldn't have to go looking for progress. Linear's Pulse is a feed of project and initiative updates, and it can send you a summary in your Linear inbox every weekday or once a week, arriving around 6am local time. You can even click Play and have the summary read aloud on your commute.


A few setup tips:


-


Pick **weekly** if you mostly track strategy, **daily** if you're closely involved in a launch.


-


Subscribe to the projects and teams you care about, so your summary covers the right work.


-


Create a private custom feed for the initiatives you own.


## 4. Respond to risk, not to noise


When an update says "at risk" or "off track," that's your moment to engage. Linear suggests leaders comment and offer help on at-risk projects. A short note like "What do you need from me to get this back on track?" does more than a status meeting.


Everything else, the individual issue churn, the comment threads, the daily back-and-forth, is noise at your level. If you find yourself reading issue comments to understand status, it's a sign the project updates aren't doing their job yet. Fix the update habit rather than going deeper.


## 5. Know what's waiting on you


Here's the part Linear alone can't solve. Some of the most important things in Linear are blocked on *you* : a decision on scope, a sign-off on a spec, a call on whether to cut a feature to hit a date. Those don't always look different from any other issue, and they're easy to miss when they're one notification among dozens.


Treat these like any other commitment. Keep a running list of what your team is waiting on from you, and clear it every day. (Our guide on how to keep track of follow-ups at work covers a simple system for this.)


## 6. Bring Linear into your daily priorities with BOND


The deeper problem is that Linear is one source among many. The engineering blocker that needs you lives in Linear. The customer escalation that explains why lives in email. The debate about the fix is in Slack. And the decision gets made in a meeting. If each lives in its own app, you're the one stitching them together.


BOND connects to Linear alongside Gmail or Outlook, Calendar, Slack, Notion, meeting notes from tools like Granola and more. It reads across all of them and keeps a single self-updating to-do list, ranked P0 to P3, of what actually needs you.


For Linear, that means:


-


**Blockers that need you surface automatically.** A decision waiting on you in Linear shows up on your list next to the email and Slack threads that relate to it.


-


**Slipping work gets flagged.** BOND's morning brief tells you what's on track, what's slipping and who's waiting on you, across engineering and the rest of the company.


-


**Meetings come with context.** Before a product review or a one-on-one with your engineering lead, BOND preps you with what's open in Linear and what was promised last time.


-


**Priorities stay accurate.** BOND learns what matters to you over time, so a launch blocker ranks above routine issue updates and it cuts through the noise.


It's the same job a great chief of staff does: keep the leader informed about what matters across every team, without making them chase it.


## 7. Use Linear in your meetings, not instead of them


Finally, put Linear to work in the meetings you already have.


-


**Weekly leadership meeting:** review the Initiatives view together for five minutes. Talk only about yellow, red and gray.


-


**One-on-ones with engineering leads:** open their projects' latest updates before the call and start with "What's the biggest risk right now?"


-


**Product reviews:** ask for decisions to be recorded in Linear so there's a single record of what was agreed.


That keeps Linear as the source of truth while you spend your time on judgment calls, not status-gathering. If every project feels urgent, our guide on how to prioritize tasks when everything is P0 can help you sort it out.

## FAQ


**Is Linear for executives or just engineers?**


Both, if executives use it at the right level. Leaders get the most from initiatives, project health and Pulse summaries rather than individual issues. That gives you an accurate view of progress without getting pulled into day-to-day engineering work.


**How do I track engineering progress in Linear?**


Use Initiatives to group projects around company goals, and ask project leads to post regular project updates with a health status. The Initiatives view then shows which goals are on track, at risk or off track at a glance.


**What is Linear Pulse?**


Pulse is a feed of project and initiative updates in Linear. You can read it in the sidebar or receive a daily or weekly summary in your Linear inbox, which can also be played as audio.


**How can I see what's blocked on me in Linear?**


Watch your Linear inbox for mentions and assigned issues, and ask your team to tag you directly on decisions. To see Linear blockers alongside everything else that needs you, connect Linear to BOND, which adds them to one prioritized to-do list.


**How often should engineering teams post project updates?**


Weekly is a good default for most projects. During a critical launch, more frequent updates can help, as long as they stay short.


**Can I get Linear updates in Slack?**


Linear integrates with Slack for notifications and updates. If you want Linear priorities combined with your email and meetings, BOND brings them together and can surface them directly in Slack.
